visuals.alt: A short visual summary of Career Options After MA.
visuals.caption: Key points at a glance.
visuals.heading: Real Question After an MA

items.text: "What do I do with an MA" is not really about the subject anymore.
Compare by runway and risk first, subject and pay second.
Do not pick a door by prestige or by what a relative did.
Academia and civil services both ask for years of low or no income before any payoff.
A PhD without a guaranteed post, or a UPSC attempt with a roughly 0.1% overall selection ratio, both carry a genuine chance of no payoff after years of effort.
Many MA graduates run a corporate or teaching job while preparing for NET or a State PSC exam in parallel.
History, political science, sociology, and public administration optionals genuinely overlap with the syllabus.
A completed PhD funded by JRF, ICSSR, or another fellowship is a real credential, but permanent assistant professor vacancies open on their own schedule, not on your graduation date.

visuals.heading: 4 Doors, Compared

rows: Corporate, policy, and industry roles
People who want to start earning within months and are willing to add one visible, market-facing skill on top of the MA.

Entry-level pay is often modest (roughly Rs 3-6 LPA) without a multiplier skill, but the pay ceiling and speed to first income both beat the other three doors, and that same skill layer opens a path to independent, scalable work later.
Teaching (school PGT/TGT, or college via NET)
People who want structured hours, direct classroom work, and a path that starts paying sooner than research or civil services.
School PGT posts typically pay Rs 30,000-55,000 a month in government schools; private schools often pay less. College teaching needs NET or a PhD first.
Academia and research (NET, JRF, PhD)
People who want to keep working inside the subject itself and are fine with a slow, funded runway before a stable salary.
JRF stipend runs roughly Rs 37,000-42,000 a month; a PhD typically takes 3-6 years; a permanent assistant professor post is not guaranteed even after NET and a PhD.
Civil services (UPSC, State PSC)
People who want the widest generalist government career and can fund 1-3 serious attempts without needing income immediately.
The overall UPSC CSE selection ratio was roughly 0.1% in the 2025 cycle. State PSCs have softer odds but far lower pay and slower recruitment cycles.

blocks.heading: Real Cost and Timeline Map
blocks.sourceSectionTitle: The real cost and timeline map

rows: NET preparation and attempt (subject-specific, MA is direct eligibility)
Usually 6-12 months of focused prep alongside or after the MA. Exam fee is modest; the real cost is time and, for some, coaching material.
JRF-funded PhD (if NET clears the JRF cutoff)
Typically 3-6 years, funded at roughly Rs 37,000-42,000 a month through the JRF stipend, rising after the second year.
ICSSR Doctoral Fellowship (if JRF is not cleared but NET is)
A strictly two-year term, funded at roughly Rs 20,000 a month plus an annual contingency grant, open mainly to social science and humanities scholars.
UPSC or State PSC preparation, if you go the civil services route
Coaching and materials commonly run Rs 1.5-3 lakh per prep year in a coaching hub, on top of foregone income of roughly Rs 3-6 lakh a year, across 1-3 realistic attempts.
State-level PGT/TGT or CTET-linked teaching recruitment
Exam-to-posting timelines vary by state, but this is generally the fastest exam-gated route to a first stable paycheck on this list, often within a year of clearing the recruitment exam.
A corporate certification or portfolio layer (HR, content, data, research methods)
Usually 2-6 months and a few thousand rupees to a low lakh, depending on the certification, and often the single fastest route to a first paycheck of all six rows here.

visuals.heading: Give the Test As Long

items.text: A PhD is always a safe, respectable choice.
Teaching is the fallback if nothing else works.
Government job or bust, private jobs are a downgrade.

blocks.heading: SSC, Banking, and PSU Exams Beyond UPSC

items.text: SSC CGL: opens central government roles across ministries and departments (Assistant, Inspector, and similar grades) to any postgraduate, with a shorter, more predictable prep cycle than UPSC CSE.

Bank PO and specialist officer exams (IBPS PO, SBI PO, RBI Grade B): accept any postgraduate degree, pay a structured, rising salary from day one, and generally have better odds than UPSC CSE, though still competitive.
PSU recruitment through non-technical hiring tracks: several public-sector undertakings run their own postgraduate-eligible drives for roles such as HR, corporate communications, and administration.
State-level Group B/C exams: often overlooked next to UPSC and the flagship State PSC exam, but genuinely faster to a paycheck and open to any MA subject.

blocks.heading: Sit One Real Past NET or UPSC

items.text: Ask one person already inside your target door, a JRF scholar, a PGT teacher, a State PSC officer, or a corporate hire in your field, what an ordinary week actually looks like, not the highlight-reel version.
Apply for one real opening in the corporate or teaching lane even while academia or civil services stays your first choice, so you have live market feedback instead of a theory.
